newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Tennis-Becker and Sampras chase another showdown.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Tennis-Becker and Sampras chase another showdown.

text.p: World number one Pete Sampras heads into next week's Australian Open with defending champion Boris Becker looming as the greatest threat to his bid for a second title.
After fellow-American Andre Agassi's challenge faded last season Sampras locked horns with Becker in a rivalry that engrossed tennis followers as 1996 drew to a close.
Sampras, the top seed in Melbourne, lost to Becker in the Stuttgart tournament final before rallying to defeat the German in an epic five-set ATP Tour World Championship final in Hanover in November.
The pair have emerged in opposite halves of the draw at the Australian Open and the only time they can meet at the National Tennis Centre is in the final on January 26.

Sampras, who is chasing his ninth grand slam win and a repeat of his 1994 Australian triumph, has declared himself physically and mentally ready, a sharp contrast to last year when he fell early to Australia's Mark Philippoussis after complaining about the lingering effects of influenza.

"I was very tired and I came down here sick last time. But this year I've had a good break, I've got here ready and eager to go," Sampras told reporters at the warm-up Kooyong Classic exibition event, where he lost in the final to compatriot Michael Chang on Saturday.

When Agassi, who is avoiding the championship this year, began his decline with a failed, lacklustre defence of his Australian Open crown, Becker emerged to relaunch his career with victory in Melbourne last January, ending a barren spell of five years without a grand slam win.
Becker, seeded sixth and the elder statesman of tennis following the retirement of Swede Stefan Edberg, will face Spaniard Carlos Moya in the first round.
Moya, a claycourt specialist, has shown outstanding form on the faster Rebound Ace hardcourt, losing to Britain's Tim Henman in the Sydney International ATP final on Saturday.
"I have seen enough of Carlos to know what a good player he is," Becker said, referring to his loss to Moya in last year's Paris Open in their only previous meeting.
Becker has benefitted from the withdrawal of world number four Yevgeny Kafelnikov from his section of the draw after the Russian broke a bone in his hand while training on Thursday.
But he still faces a possible semifinal against world number two and second seed Chang in what would be a repeat of last year's final.
Chang will face qualifier Kris Goossens of Belgium in the first round, while Sampras will tackle another little known qualifier Dinu Pescariu.
Indeed, such is Pescariu's lowly ranking and meagre tour record, Sampras admitted he had never even heard of his Romanian opponent.
In the women's singles, Steffi Graf could face the biggest threat to her campaign to win a fifth Australian Open title from a courtroom in her native Germany.
The judge in the highly publicised tax trial of her father, Peter, has said he expects a ruling on the case on January 24, the Friday before the final weekend of the grand slam.
The case centres on allegations of avoiding tax on millions of dollars of the world number one's earnings.

Graf, who is chasing her fifth Australian Open crown after being absent last year because of injury, remains under investigation herself in the affair, which has caused her enormous emotional stress in the past year.
On the court rather than in it, however, there appears little to concern Graf after rival Monica Seles was forced to stay away with a broken finger, ruining her chances of defending her Open title.

With second seed Arantxa Sanchez Vicario seemingly consigned to a prominent role in the supporting cast after so many grand slam final defeats in the past, it has been left to Swiss teenager Martina Hingis to generate some excitement.
Fourth-seeded Hingis, who proved her readiness by winning the Sydney International on Saturday, has already beaten Graf and shows increasing signs of maturity beyond her 16 years.
As in the men's singles, the two most marketable players have been drawn apart, creating a mouth-watering prospect for tournament organisers and fans alike.
-- Sydney Newsroom 61-2 9373-1800
